title: Hellenistic schools: Stoics, Epicureans, Skeptics
note: After Aristotle, schools offered whole ways of life aimed at happiness. Stoics held that virtue is the only good and that we should live in agreement with a rational nature. Epicureans held that the goal is pleasure, understood as freedom from pain and fear. Skeptics suspended judgment to find peace of mind.

read.title: Three roads to peace
text: After Alexander's conquests, Greek philosophy became a guide to living well in an uncertain world. Three schools gave rival answers.

The Stoics taught that the cosmos is ordered by divine reason, the logos, and that human beings share in it. Virtue, the excellence of reason, is the only true good. Health, wealth, and reputation are preferred, and it is reasonable to pursue them, but they are not good in themselves, because they can be misused. Since passions such as fear and envy rest on false judgments about what matters, the wise person can be free of them. Epictetus summed it up: some things are up to us, our judgments and choices, and the rest are not.

Epicurus held that the goal of life is pleasure, but by pleasure he meant mainly the absence of pain in the body and disturbance in the soul. Simple food, friends, and clear thinking supply it. Since the soul is made of atoms that scatter at death, death is not something we will ever experience, so fearing it is pointless.
The skeptics noticed that equally strong arguments can be found on both sides of most questions. Pyrrhonists responded by suspending judgment and reported that tranquility followed.
